claims.text: The equiatomic FeNiCrMn alloy is initially a single-phase FCC solid solution.
The FeNiCrMn alloy has a random atomic distribution.
The simulated initial state contains a controlled density of vacancy clusters.
The yield strength of equiatomic FeNiCrMn is insensitive to strain rate between 10^8 and 10^10 s^-1.
Shockley partial dislocations nucleate heterogeneously at pre-existing vacancy clusters.
Shockley-partial nucleation at vacancy clusters is athermal within the simulated temperature and strain-rate window.
The nucleation barrier is dominated by local chemical disorder, lattice distortion, and unstable stacking-fault energy rather than thermal activation.
Athermal nucleation makes yielding depend on the immediate stress state rather than time-dependent diffusion or dislocation annihilation, producing strain-rate-insensitive yield strength.
Shockley partial dislocations generate intrinsic stacking faults during deformation of FeNiCrMn.
The deformation produces neither twinning nor a phase transformation.
Dislocation nucleation will occur exclusively at vacancy clusters regardless of strain rate.
The <11-1>-oriented FeNiCrMn sample will exhibit a higher maximum yield-stress peak than the <110>-oriented sample.
The higher predicted yield stress for <11-1> results from a higher critical resolved shear stress needed to nucleate partials on a {111} plane.
The <11-1> alignment maximizes resolved shear stress on the critical slip plane relative to the <110> alignment.
Yield strength and yield strain decrease monotonically as temperature increases.
The Bonny et al. potential can represent stacking-fault energetics relevant to the proposed simulations.
HCP-like regions can be identified as intrinsic stacking faults by demonstrating that they are planar defects rather than three-dimensional regions with a distinct transformed lattice.
Extreme deformation of equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi can produce amorphous regions.

contradictions.description: The predicted higher applied yield stress for <11-1> is attributed to a higher required critical resolved shear stress, while the mechanism also says <11-1> maximizes the resolved shear stress relative to <110>. Greater resolved shear per unit applied stress would normally favor earlier yielding unless an independently larger nucleation barrier is established; no such quantitative reconciliation is provided.
The intervention gives a lower temperature limit of 10 mK, whereas the conditions give 1 mK.
